questions.q: State the definition of a set as per the NCERT textbook and identify the two key adjectives used to describe the collection.
questions.a: A set is a well-defined collection of distinct objects. The two key adjectives are **well-defined** (membership rule is objective and unambiguous) and **distinct** (no repetition of elements). A wrong answer (e.g., "a collection of objects" without the adjectives) reveals the student misses the *defining* feature that separates sets from arbitrary groups.

questions.q: Explain in your own words why "the collection of all intelligent students in Class 11" is **not** a set, but "the collection of all students in Class 11 who scored above 90% in the Term 1 exam" **is** a set.
questions.a: "Intelligent" is subjective—different teachers/parents have different criteria, so membership cannot be decided objectively. "Scored above 90%" is a precise, verifiable rule: given any student, we check their marksheet and get a definite yes/no. A wrong answer (e.g., "both are sets because they describe groups") shows the student confuses *description* with *well-defined criterion*.

questions.q: Given the set A = {x : x is a letter in the word "BANANA"}, write A in roster form and state the cardinal number n(A). Then, determine whether 'N' ∈ A and 'B' ∉ A are true or false.
questions.a: A = {B, A, N} (distinct letters only). n(A) = 3. 'N' ∈ A is **True** (N appears in BANANA). 'B' ∉ A is **False** (B is the first letter). A wrong roster form {B, A, N, A, N, A} reveals the student ignores "distinct"; a wrong cardinality reveals they counted repetitions; wrong ∈/∉ reveals confusion about membership vs. non-membership.

questions.q: Compare the two collections: (i) C = {x : x is a root of x² - 5x + 6 = 0} and (ii) D = {x : x is a "difficult" chapter in the NCERT Class 11 Maths textbook}. Analyze which is a set and why, focusing on the *nature of the defining property*.
questions.a: C is a set: the equation has exactly two roots (2 and 3), verifiable by any student. D is **not** a set: "difficult" is relative—one student finds Trigonometry hard, another finds Calculus hard; no universal rule exists. A wrong answer (e.g., "both are sets because they have elements") shows the student cannot distinguish *objective mathematical property* from *subjective human judgment*.

questions.q: A student argues: "The collection of all real numbers between 0 and 1 is not a set because it has infinitely many elements and we cannot list them." Evaluate this claim and defend your judgment using the definition of a set.
questions.a: The claim is **false**. A set does **not** require listability (roster form); it only requires a well-defined membership rule. The rule "x ∈ R and 0 < x < 1" is perfectly objective—any real number can be tested. The set is infinite but well-defined (it is the open interval (0,1)). A wrong evaluation reveals the student conflates *finiteness/representability* with *well-definedness*.

questions.q: Create your own real-life example of a collection that **looks like** a set but fails the "well-defined" test due to a subtle ambiguity. State the collection, the ambiguous term, and rewrite it to make it a valid set.
questions.a: Example: "The collection of all *tall* buildings in Mumbai." Ambiguous term: "tall" (no fixed height threshold). Rewritten set: "The collection of all buildings in Mumbai with height > 100 meters." A poor answer (e.g., "collection of good movies" without identifying the ambiguous term or fixing it) shows the student cannot *construct* well-defined criteria, only recognize them.
